steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,650 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,880/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk through this and tell you what’s deductible, which method likely makes sense, and what forms you’ll need. A couple clarifying questions up front so I give exact guidance:
- Is the $5,100 “student loan interest” the amount you paid in 2024, or is that interest paid in prior years (2018–2021)? Only interest paid in 2024 can be deducted on your 2024 return.
- The $540 “unreimbursed expenses” — were these business expenses related to your photography (supplies, travel, software, etc.) or employee/unreimbursed work expenses? (Employee unreimbursed expenses are not deductible; business expenses are deductible on Schedule C.)
- Do you rent your home? (You said you pay $1,880/month, so I assume yes.) Does that rent include utilities, or are utilities billed separately?

Assuming you rent and the $540 are photography business expenses and the $5,100 question is clarified below, here’s how things look.

What you should report as income
- W-2 wages: $96,500 (report on Form 1040 as wages).
- Self-employment (photography): $16,300 — report on Schedule C (profit/loss from business).
- Interest/dividend income: $2,650 (Capital One 360) + $420 (Merrill Edge) = $3,070 — report as taxable interest/dividends (you’ll get 1099-INT / 1099-DIV). Because total interest/ordinary dividends > $1,500, you will likely need Schedule B.

Self-employment items and self-employment tax
- You’ll report your business revenue and deductible business expenses on Schedule C. Business expenses would include the home-office allocation (see below) and the $540 if those are true business expenses (supplies, equipment, software, mileage for business, advertising, etc.).
- Net profit from Schedule C is subject to self-employment tax (Social Security + Medicare). You use Schedule SE to compute this. You can deduct one-half of the self-employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (reduces AGI).

Home office treatment
- You said 120 sq ft exclusive use, total home 740 sq ft. Business-use percentage = 120 / 740 ≈ 16.22%.
- Two methods:
  - Actual-expense method (likely better here): allocate a percentage of rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, and other allowable home expenses to the business. Example using only rent: annual rent = $1,880 × 12 = $22,560. Rent portion = 16.22% × $22,560 ≈ $3,658. That $3,658 would be a deductible business expense on Schedule C (reduce self-employment income).
    - Because you rent, you generally cannot claim depreciation on the home structure (depreciation applies when you own the home).
    - If utilities are separate, you can allocate their percentage as well and increase the deduction.
    - If you use the actual-expense method, you normally complete Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and attach it to Schedule C.
  - Simplified method: $5.00 per square foot up to 300 sq ft. For 120 sq ft that’s $600. You do not use Form 8829 with the simplified method; you claim the deduction directly on Schedule C.
- Based on rent alone, the actual method (~$3,658) will be larger than the simplified method ($600). If utilities or other allocable costs exist, actual-method advantage increases. So actual method is likely better for you. Keep lease, rent receipts, photos/measurements, and records showing exclusive use.

Student loan interest
- The maximum student loan interest deduction is $2,500 per year (adjustment to income), but it phases out at higher MAGI (so eligibility depends on your modified adjusted gross income). You also can only deduct interest you actually paid in the tax year (not amounts paid in prior years).
- If the $5,100 is interest paid in prior years, it is not deductible for your 2024 return. If you paid $5,100 in 2024, the maximum deductible on 2024 return is $2,500 subject to income phaseouts. You’ll receive Form 1098-E from your loan servicer if you paid interest in the year.

Charitable contributions
- Your $1,500 cash gift to Salvation Army is a qualified charitable contribution (you have a receipt). Charitable gifts are deductible only if you itemize.
- For 2024 single filers, the standard deduction will almost certainly exceed $1,500 alone, so itemizing only for the $1,500 likely isn’t beneficial. (See “Itemize vs Standard” below.)

Unreimbursed employee expenses
- If the $540 is unreimbursed employee expenses (for a W-2 job), those are not deductible for tax years after 2017 under current law (suspended miscellaneous itemized deductions). If they are business expenses for your photography, they belong on Schedule C.

Itemize vs. standard deduction
- You’ll compare your itemized deductions (charitable contributions, mortgage interest, state/local taxes, property taxes, medical expenses above threshold, etc.) to the standard deduction for single filers.
- Based on the numbers you gave, the only clear itemizable amount is $1,500 charitable contribution. Unless you have other itemizable items (large state/local taxes, mortgage interest, big medical expenses, etc.), the standard deduction will be larger than your itemized total. So you will almost certainly take the standard deduction.
- Note: home office deductions are not itemized deductions — they are business deductions (Schedule C) and reduce your AGI via lower business profit and lower self-employment tax — so they don’t affect the itemize vs. standard decision directly.

Forms you’ll likely need to file
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return).
- Schedule 1 (for adjustments to income) — includes half of self-employment tax, and student loan interest deduction (if allowed).
- Schedule B — if taxable interest/dividends total more than $1,500 (your total $3,070 triggers Schedule B).
- Schedule C — to report the photography income and business expenses (including home office deduction by dollar amount).
- Schedule SE — to calculate self-employment tax.
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual home-office expense method (allocate actual rent/utilities). If you use the simplified method, you do not file 8829.
- 1099s/1098s you’ll attach/keep: 1099-INT (Capital One), 1099-DIV or 1099-B (Merrill Edge), 1099-NEC (if any client issued you one), and Form 1098-E (student loan interest) if you receive it.
- Form 1040-ES — if you need to make quarterly estimated tax payments during the year (you’ll want to pay estimated taxes if you expect to owe tax from self-employment income to avoid penalties).

Recordkeeping and practical notes
- Keep receipts / documentation for the home-office measurement, lease and rent payments, utilities, business expenses, charitable gift receipt, and any 1099/1098 forms.
- If you expect to owe taxes because of self-employment income, consider making quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040-ES).
- Half of the self-employment tax is an “above the line” deduction — that helps reduce your AGI.

Estimated numbers (rough)
- Total gross income ≈ $115,870 (96,500 + 16,300 + 3,070).
- If you take actual home-office rent portion ≈ $3,658 and deduct $540 business expenses, net SE income ≈ $12,102.
- Estimated self-employment tax on that ≈ $1,710; half (≈ $855) is an adjustment to income.
- Student loan interest deduction (if eligible) is capped at $2,500.
- Itemized deductions based on info you gave are only $1,500 — so standard deduction will almost certainly be better.

Next steps I can help with
- If you want, I can prepare a checklist of exact documents to gather and a step-by-step filing plan.
- I can draft an email to a tax preparer summarizing your numbers and questions (or forward your 1099s to a preparer) if you’d like.
- Answer follow-ups after you confirm whether the $5,100 is interest paid in 2024 and whether the $540 are business expenses.

I’m not a CPA — this is general guidance. If you want a definitive answer for complicated phaseouts (student loan interest phaseout and how your AGI affects it) or to optimize deductions, I recommend a licensed tax preparer or CPA. Would you like me to prepare the documents checklist or draft an email to a tax preparer now?
